creative.body:
If you're going 3, 4, even 5 days between bowel movements since you started Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro or Zepbound — it's not because you need more fiber, more water, or more salads.

My name is Dr. Rebecca Marsh.

I'm a gastroenterologist, and I've spent the last eighteen years specializing in gut motility disorders, which is the medical term for the speed at which food moves through your digestive system. It's a quiet corner of medicine. Most of my training was for patients with diabetic gastroparesis, post-surgical motility complications, and the rare hereditary motility syndromes that affect maybe one in ten thousand people. I expected to spend my career in that quiet corner.

Then GLP-1 medication went mainstream.

I'm writing this for the people on a GLP-1 medication who have quietly accepted the bloating, the four-day stretches, the pants that stop fitting by dinner, and the shot-day dread as the cost of finally losing the weight.

If you'll hear me out, I can explain something the doctor who wrote your prescription never had the time to. Something that every online article, every Reddit thread, and every well-meaning "have you tried more fiber" comment has missed completely.

Here's what this is about.

Over the last three years in my practice, I've watched the same story play out again and again.

A patient starts the shot.

The weight starts coming off.

Within a few weeks, their digestion falls apart.

These are patients who have done everything they've been told to do.

Who have doubled their fiber.

Who are drinking so much water they can't sleep through the night.

Who have packed every meal with leafy greens.

Who have tried Miralax, Metamucil, Dulcolax, psyllium husk, magnesium citrate, three different probiotics, and a drawerful of digestive enzymes.

And who still wake up bloated, distended, and unable to pass anything for four, five, sometimes six days at a stretch.

I've had patients in my exam room in tears, telling me they've started skipping meals not because they aren't hungry but because the pressure of food sitting on top of food on top of food has become unbearable.

I've had patients tell me they've stopped going out to eat with their families because they don't trust their bodies to make it through a meal without the bloating turning into something worse.

I've had patients who came to me already on the verge of quitting the medication. Patients who had lost forty, fifty, sixty pounds. Patients whose blood sugar had finally normalized. Patients whose joints had stopped hurting for the first time in a decade. And who were ready to throw the pen in the trash because the constipation and the bloating had become more miserable than the weight itself ever was.

At some point I started to understand these patients didn't need more fiber.

They didn't need another laxative.

They needed someone to explain what was actually happening to their stomach the moment that medication entered their system.

After three years of watching this exact pattern repeat, and months of digging through the research behind it, I found that explanation.

And more importantly, an approach that works with the slowed stomach instead of piling more food on top of it.

What it consists of is a formula built around the one mechanism every piece of dietary advice has been ignoring: the speed at which your stomach is now moving.

The reason you're constipated and bloated on your GLP-1 has nothing to do with what you're eating.

It has to do with how slowly your stomach is now releasing what you eat into the rest of your system.

Patients who have tried this approach tell me they have their first easy, unassisted bowel movement within ten to fourteen days.

Some within the first week.

After months of four-day stretches, bloating that made their jeans unwearable by dinner, and shot days spent dreading the next forty-eight hours, that kind of change is the difference between staying on the medication and giving up on it.

Let me explain what's actually happening.

GLP-1 medications work by slowing your stomach down.

That isn't a side effect. That's the medication doing exactly what it was designed to do, holding food in your stomach longer so you feel full on less.

The weight loss depends on that slowdown.

But here's what nobody explained when you were handed the prescription.

Your stomach is now emptying at a fraction of the speed it used to.

Food that would normally leave your stomach in two hours is now sitting there for five, six, sometimes eight.

Every meal lands on top of the meal before it.

Nothing is flowing through. Everything is stacking up.

And here is the part that explains why every piece of dietary advice you've been given has made it worse rather than better.

Fiber. Water. Salads. Vegetables. Psyllium husk. Metamucil.

Every single one of them is food. And food requires a moving stomach to do anything for you.

Fiber does not fix a slowed stomach. Fiber added to a stomach that has stopped releasing its contents just joins the pile that is already sitting there.

Which is why the more fiber you added, the worse the bloating got.

Which is why the extra water only made you feel fuller, not more regular.

Which is why the salads produced gas and pressure instead of relief.

You weren't failing to follow the advice correctly.

The advice itself was aimed at a problem you don't have.

You don't have a fiber deficiency.

Your stomach has been slowed to a crawl by the medication, and every recommendation you've been handed was designed for a stomach that empties in two hours. Yours, as it was before the shot.

I want to spend a minute on why this is happening at the cellular level, because once you understand it, the rest of this letter will make a different kind of sense.

Your stomach has its own electrical pacemaker. It generates a rhythm of three contractions per minute that pushes food along. That rhythm is governed by a hormone called motilin, which your gut releases between meals to keep things moving.

GLP-1 medication suppresses motilin. That is part of how it works. The medication binds to receptors in your gut, slows the release of motilin, and the contraction rhythm drops. The pacemaker is still there. It is just being told to take it slow.

When food sits in a stomach that is contracting at half speed, two things happen.

First, the food begins to ferment. Bacteria that normally live in your gut, specifically bacteria that thrive in the small intestine when food has been sitting too long, get a longer feeding window than they were ever designed to have. They produce sulfur compounds, methane, and hydrogen as byproducts.

That is what your bloating actually is. It is not water retention. It is not a food intolerance. It is the gas your own gut bacteria are producing because the food is sitting in your stomach for three to four times longer than it is supposed to.

Second, the food that finally does move out of your stomach reaches your colon hours late and in a state your colon was not built to receive. Your colon expects partially-broken-down food at a steady, predictable rate. What it is now getting is dumped in irregular waves with too much fermentation already in it.

Your colon, in response, slows down its own contractions. It is trying to give your body time to figure out what just arrived. The result is constipation that does not respond to colon-targeted laxatives, because the colon is not the problem. The colon is downstream of the problem.

This is what every piece of dietary advice you have been given has missed.

The standard advice was written for a normal stomach. The standard advice tells you to feed a colon that is sluggish from too little fiber. Your colon is not sluggish from too little fiber. Your colon is sluggish because your stomach is sending it signals six hours late.

The solution is not more food at the colon. The solution is to work with the slowed stomach so that what reaches the colon arrives the way the colon expects it.

Your stomach does not need more food. It needs to start moving what is already sitting there.

There's a compound in celery juice called apigenin.

If you have not heard of it, you are not alone. It is one of the more under-studied flavonoids in modern nutritional science, despite being one of the more abundant compounds in a category of vegetables we have all been eating for centuries.

The research on apigenin shows it supports gastric motility at the exact point where GLP-1s have slowed it down. It does not override the medication. It does not force contractions or create urgency the way a laxative does. It helps the stomach begin doing what it has stopped doing on its own.

The mechanism is well-documented. Apigenin acts on the receptors that govern smooth muscle contraction in the stomach wall. It does not bypass the GLP-1 medication. It works at a different layer of the same system, gently restoring some of the motility tone the medication has suppressed, without compromising the slowdown that produces the weight loss.

That distinction matters. It is the reason this approach can work for someone on a GLP-1 without undermining the medication itself.

The food that has been stacking up finally moves.

The bloating releases.

The pressure that has been building for days starts to come down.

And once the system is flowing again, a small targeted amount of soluble prebiotic fiber, working downstream, inside a digestive tract that's actually functioning, does what fiber was always supposed to do in the first place.

There is a third piece I want to mention, because it addresses the part of the GLP-1 experience nobody likes to talk about.

The sulfur burps.

If you have had them, you know exactly what I mean. The gassy reflux that tastes like rotten eggs. The kind of burp that you cannot predict, that you cannot suppress, and that makes you afraid to be in a meeting or on a date or in a car with your mother-in-law.

Those burps are a direct product of the fermentation I described earlier. They are the sulfur compounds that bacteria in your stalled stomach are producing. They smell exactly like what they are.

Chlorophyllin is a stabilized form of chlorophyll, the pigment that makes green plants green. It binds to sulfur compounds at the molecular level. It does not mask the smell. It neutralizes the source. The bacteria can keep producing whatever they are producing, but the chlorophyllin chemically deactivates the byproducts before they reach the back of your throat.

When you put apigenin and chlorophyllin and a targeted dose of soluble prebiotic fiber together, you are addressing the three things actually happening in a slowed stomach.

The motility itself.

The fermentation byproducts.

And the downstream support for the colon once the system is moving again.

That is the approach.

The striking thing about this, once you understand the mechanism, is how simple the fix becomes.

No complicated protocol. No elimination diet. No prescription with new side effects that create a fresh set of problems.

Two gummies in the morning. That's all.

Picture buttoning your jeans at the end of the day without having to unbutton them again by dinner.

Sitting through a meal out without calculating how many hours you have before the bloating hits.

Waking up on shot day and not already dreading the next two days.

Stepping on the scale and seeing the weight coming off, without the misery that used to come with it.

I want to walk you through what I have actually seen happen with patients who started this approach. Not in a clinical trial setting. In my practice, with the people sitting across from me at follow-up visits.

The first week, most people notice the burps stop. The chlorophyllin works fast. The fermentation gases that were reaching your throat get neutralized within a few days. That is usually the first sign that something is shifting.

The second week, the bloating starts to ease. Not gone. Eased. The pressure under your ribs gets lighter. You start being able to sit through a full dinner without needing to change into elastic pants afterward.

By the end of the second week, most people have their first unassisted bowel movement.

I want to spend a sentence on what unassisted means. It means you woke up and went, the way you used to before any of this started. No magnesium the night before. No Miralax cleanout. No emergency Dulcolax. No suppository. Just a body doing what bodies are supposed to do.

For a lot of my patients, that morning is the first time in three or four months their body has done that on its own. Several of them have texted me from the bathroom. One emailed me a single word, which I will not include here, but which made me laugh out loud at my desk.

By week four, the pattern starts to feel reliable. Daily or every-other-day movements. Bloating that does not return by dinner. Shot day comes and goes without the dread.

By month two, most people are not thinking about their gut anymore. They are losing weight. They are stepping on the scale. They are putting on clothes that fit. The medication is doing what it was supposed to do, and the constipation is no longer the price.

That is what working with the slowed stomach instead of fighting it looks like in practice.

Now I want to address two questions I get from every patient before they try this.

The first question is whether this will interfere with the GLP-1 medication.

It will not. Apigenin does not bind to the GLP-1 receptor. It does not slow weight loss. It does not change appetite suppression. It works on a separate pathway, the smooth muscle motility pathway, which is where your stomach has been suppressed too far for digestion to keep up.

The medication is still doing its job. You are just no longer paying for it with a stomach that has stopped emptying.

The second question is whether this is going to cause urgency or cramping the way Miralax or magnesium citrate or Dulcolax do.

It will not. There is nothing in this formula that triggers contractions in your colon the way a stimulant laxative does. There is no osmotic agent pulling water in the way Miralax does. There is no rebound the way there is with stimulant laxatives, where your bowel becomes dependent on the stimulus to function.

This is not a laxative. It is a motility support. The difference is the difference between forcing your stomach to do something and helping it remember how to do what it used to do on its own.

My first concern in pointing patients toward any approach is safety.

The product I am referring to is called Motilli. I am not affiliated with the company. I do not have a financial relationship with them. I started recommending it to patients after I saw the formulation, read the research behind each ingredient, and watched the first handful of patients I sent to it come back with results I had not seen from any other approach.

Motilli contains no laxative compounds, no stimulants, and no ingredients that force urgency, cramping, or dependency.

It's built around apigenin from celery juice extract, chlorophyllin, and a targeted dose of soluble prebiotic fiber, three ingredients the research supports for the specific mechanism I've described.

It's delivered as a gummy. That matters more than it might sound. When you're nauseous from the shot, swallowing one more capsule is often the thing that pushes you over the edge. A capsule also requires a stomach acid environment that is actually working to break it down and release the actives. If your stomach has slowed to a crawl, capsules don't reliably dissolve, and the actives don't reliably release.

A gummy is essentially pre-dissolved. The actives release in your mouth and the upper stomach almost immediately. Two gummies go down without water, without thought, and without adding to what is already sitting in your stomach.

That is a small detail. It is also the difference, for a lot of my patients, between something that works and something they cannot tolerate.

I want to say one more thing about what this is and what it is not.

This is not a magic bullet. It is not going to make your medication work better. It is not going to accelerate your weight loss. It is not going to fix every symptom of every person who tries it.

What it is, is a way to address the specific mechanism that the GLP-1 medication has put your stomach in. It works because it is targeting the right organ for the right reason at the right depth. It is not a guess. It is the formulation that emerged when someone actually asked what is the slowed stomach missing, and built a product around the answer.

For the right patient, that approach is the difference between staying on the medication and giving up on it.

## IMPORTANT NOTE

I'm not asking you to purchase this and hope for the best.

I'm asking you to try it properly, two gummies in the morning for ninety days, and see what happens to a digestive system that is finally being worked with instead of fought against.

Motilli offers a full 90-day no-risk guarantee.

If the bloating, constipation, and shot-day misery haven't meaningfully improved in that time, you're fully covered.

No questions asked.

I don't think you'll need that guarantee. But it's there because anyone who has been told for months to "just eat more fiber" while suffering every single day since their first injection deserves to find out without risking anything further.

If you're willing to give this a proper trial, I'll simply ask you to click the link below.

You don't need to explain your history or justify your skepticism.

I understand both.

I've sat across from patients who were days away from throwing the pen in the trash. People who had already decided the weight loss wasn't worth what it was costing them.

And I've watched what happens when the stomach is finally allowed to move again.

The weight loss continues. The bloating goes. The bathroom mornings stop being a multi-day project. The medication that was working all along is finally allowed to work without dragging the rest of your life under with it.

That's why I'm writing this.

If you have read this far, you already know whether what I have described is what is happening to you. You know the four-day stretches. You know the pressure under your ribs. You know the shot-day dread. You know the elastic pants by dinner.

You also know that nothing you have tried so far has actually addressed the real problem, because nothing you have tried so far was built for the real problem.

The link is below.

Sincerely,

**Dr. Rebecca Marsh**
*Gastroenterology and GI Motility Disorders*

---

**P.S.** The advice you've been given isn't wrong for most people.

Fiber helps most people. More water helps most people. More greens, more hydration, more movement, all of it helps most people.

But most people's stomachs empty in two hours.

Yours is taking six, seven, sometimes eight.

That single variable changes everything.

Every piece of dietary advice you've been handed was built for a stomach that doesn't exist anymore. Yours, as it was before the shot.

If you've been told to "just eat more fiber" while suffering every single day since starting your medication, this is why.

And this is the approach built for the stomach you actually have right now.
